source_read: PDF pp. 102–107 (all pages; Tables 1–3 on p. 105 checked on the rendered page)

claims.note: No number in the claim comes from Measham. As far as this source goes, it fits 'disputed' and 'insufficient': it relays critics' worries (false 'shine of safety', lower deterrence, normalisation) and advocates' country-level argument that European countries with drug checking saw no rise in use or deaths, all without a controlled comparison, and its own data come from a laboratory service with a consultation, not from kits. The only data here on responses to an 'as expected' result (Table 3) show mostly 'usual amount' and no riskier intentions recorded, from an open question coded afterwards.

anchors.locator: Introduction › Controversies in drug safety testing, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Critics' concerns relayed: field testing at best gives an artificial 'shine of safety' (Winstock et al., 2001); speed–accuracy trade-offs of portable equipment; dealers using services for quality control; focus on contaminants rather than risky behaviours; limited evidence that information causes behaviour change; lower deterrence and higher appeal through perceived safety; normalisation.

anchors.locator: Introduction › Controversies in drug safety testing, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Relays Brunt (2012): two decades of Dutch testing and alerts with no perverse effect on use or drug-related deaths; no evidence that prevalence, initiation or mortality rose in European countries with drug checking compared with those without (country-level comparisons of services, not kits).

anchors.locator: Discussion › Pilot limitations and future directions, 3rd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Author argues, without data, that the service is unlikely to raise drug use and more likely deters than stimulates; calls for monitoring of unintended effects, including displacement to other drugs or alcohol reported anecdotally by some service users.

After a result matching what the drug was sold as (n = 164): usual amount 111 (67.7%), later or over a longer period 20 (12.2%), smaller amount 7 (4.3%), police disposal 15 (9.1%); coded from an open question.

claims.overstatement: (1) The lead's 'though most did not' does not hold for the festival's unexpected-result group: two thirds (30/45) handed drugs over. It holds for the festival overall (49/230 = 21%) and for the strip studies. Suggest e.g. 'most did not, except at the festival, where two thirds of those whose drug was not as sold handed drugs over'. (2) The festival comparison is 'did not match what it was sold or given as', which the paper distinguishes from what users expected after buying and perhaps trying the drug (Table 2 note); the festival sentence is worded correctly but the lead's 'unexpected' is looser. (3) The comparison is unadjusted and per primary service user (groups of about four), as the 'is associated with' wording allows.
claims.note: Recomputed: 30/45 = 66.7% (Wilson 52.1–78.6%), 15/164 = 9.1% (5.6–14.5%), difference 57.5 points (Newcombe 42.0–70.0), risk ratio 7.3; 49/230 = 21.3%; 111/164 = 67.7%; 4/45 = 8.9%: all the same as the claim. p < .01 as printed. The disposals are seen by the service (the paper calls them externally corroborated), but the author notes some people kept the rest of their supply in their tent or binned it, as the claim says. Measham's introduction relays an earlier evidence brief (Leece, 2017) with disposal rates of 4% to 76%, much wider than the claim's review figure of 0 to 10 in 100; that difference in the review evidence is worth a phrase.

anchors.extracted: Disposal for police destruction: matched sold-as 15/164 (9.1%); did not match 30/45 (66.7%); don't know (e.g. ground finds) 4/21 (19%); total 49/230 (21.3%). Note: 'matched sold as' is distinguished from what users expected after buying and possibly trying the drug.
21.3% used the disposal service after hearing the result; 66.7% vs 9.1% (p < .01) for non-matching vs matching results; onsite-acquired 27% vs offsite 14.8% (p < .05); women 24.7% vs men 19.6%.

Stated intentions coded from an open question: usual amount 111/164 (67.7%) matched vs 4/45 (8.9%) non-matched; throw it away myself 1 (0.6%) vs 4 (8.9%); return to dealer 1 vs 1; 230 primary service users.

anchors.locator: Results › Individual behavioural outcomes, 2nd paragraph (continued in right column)
anchors.extracted: Some festival-goers likely bring one dose and keep the rest in their tent for fear of arrest; some may discard unwanted drugs in a bin instead of using the disposal service.

Volunteer postgraduate chemists in an on-site laboratory (FTIR, reagent tests, mass-loss analysis); results given in 15–20 minute healthcare consultations with harm-reduction advice and the offer of a disposal service for police destruction; 230 consultations; visitors came in groups of about four.

anchors.locator: Introduction › Controversies in drug safety testing, 4th and 5th paragraphs
anchors.extracted: A review (Leece, 2017) relays disposal rates of 4% to 76%; disposal has been measured as intentions, recalled behaviour, hypothetical intentions or actual disposal right after the result, the last being the strongest and the measure used here.

claims.overstatement: None; the claim is suitably cautious. Small points: the Discussion calls the fall '95% on previous years', but only 2015 is given (described as similar to earlier years, without figures); and the changing agencies and indicators are stated as a general weakness of the pilot's meso-level data, not specifically of the admission counts.
claims.note: Recomputed: 19 to 1 is a 94.7% fall (printed 95%); admissions not classed as drug-related 59 − 19 = 40 and 50 − 1 = 49 (editors' calculation correct). 247 samples, 230 consultations, 25,000 capacity, July 2016, alerts to on-site agencies: all as stated. The admission figures are cited to two unpublished Cambridgeshire Constabulary post-event reports (Ward 2015, 2016), collated by the multi-agency harm-reduction lead. No interval or test is given. The paramedic explanation was offered by festival and partner agencies.

anchors.extracted: Festival reported a 95% fall in drug-related hospital admissions: 19 of 59 admissions in 2015 (similar to previous years) vs 1 of 50 in 2016; agencies' explanations: awareness through alerts and word of mouth, earlier presentation, and paramedics more confident treating drug-related cases on site rather than sending them to hospital.

anchors.locator: References (Ward, 2015; Ward, 2016); p. 105, Meso level impact, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Admission data usually recorded by the festival paramedical service, here collated by the multi-agency harm-reduction lead; sources are unpublished Cambridgeshire Constabulary post-event reports for 2015 and 2016.

The pilot cannot establish any contribution of the service to fewer admissions because other variables could not be controlled; still describes one drug-related admission as a 95% reduction on previous years.

anchors.locator: Discussion › Pilot limitations and future directions, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Meso-level data vary in quality, with year-to-year changes in agencies employed and indicators used; some data did not separate drug-related from other incidents or alcohol from drug intoxication.

anchors.locator: Results › Meso level impact, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Daily updates of results to all on-site agencies and targeted alerts; no drug-related deaths at the festival in 2016, a year with six at UK festivals (highest on record); deaths at festivals rare and multifactorial, so admissions are proposed as the better measure.

anchors.locator: Abstract; p. 104 Methods 3rd paragraph; p. 103 Controversies 6th paragraph
anchors.extracted: 247 substances analysed in an on-site laboratory over four days, results returned in 230 consultations (results not collected for 17), reaching about 900 people; 25,000-capacity festival, July 2016; first UK on-site service, not advertised in advance.

reporting_issues.note: The reconstruction is consistent with every printed sex percentage (77 women, 153 men). Fisher p = 0.397 for disposal and 0.208 for first use, as stated.
Place-of-purchase reconstruction (111 onsite, 115 offsite) reproduces 27%, 12% and 14.8%; Fisher p = 0.0068 and 0.032.

risk_of_bias.note: Agree with ROBINS-I, critical overall for effects on consumption or admissions, and with the domain judgments. Two points for the adjudicator. (1) The card is filed as design case-series, for which METHODS §5.3 lists no instrument, but appraises it with ROBINS-I under a topic instruction; worth checking against scripts/rob_vocab.py. (2) For the observed disposal-by-result association, worded as an association, the observed outcome makes the evidence firmer than 'critical' suggests, as the card's reasoning says.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the 95% fall is reported under results before the concession that the pilot cannot attribute it. The abstract's 'one in six moderated' and the claims that disposals reduce harm and that a feedback loop to suppliers occurred go beyond the data.
